title: Wieslaw Duda inquest: Family called Peel police hours before shooting death
subtitle: In the hours before he was shot dead inside his car by police, a member of Wieslaw Duda's family called Peel Regional Police, concerned about his behaviour, a coroner's inquest into the 2010 death heard Monday.
article: Just hours before Wieslaw Duda was shot dead by Toronto police inside his car, a member of his family called Peel Regional Police, concerned about his behaviour, a coroner's inquest into the death revealed Monday.

It was the first day of testimony into the April 2010 fatal shooting of Duda, a 49-year-old Mississauga man who family said suffered from schizophrenia. Duda died in a hail of bullets inside his car near Toronto's Port Lands area, after leading police on a brief car chase.

The coroner's inquest - mandatory in the case of police-involved fatal shootings - is just the latest examination of how Toronto police react to people experiencing a mental crisis, and will once again put the microscope to when and how police use lethal force.

For Duda's family, including his two children, his mother and three sisters, it has been a long four and a half years, said Kurt Bergmanis, one of the lawyer's representing the family. They have many unanswered questions, and see the inquest as a "fact-finding mission."
"There's been very little, if any, information imparted to the family, and our job is to walk away knowing a little more than what we came with," he said outside coroner's court Monday.

It is likely to be the only time the finer details surrounding Duda's death will be heard in court: an investigation by the Special Investigations Unit, which probes all police incidents involving death or serious injury, ruled shortly after the death that there were no grounds to lay criminal charges against the officers involved.

On Monday, during a brief address to court, lawyer for the coroner Michael Blain revealed that in the hours before Duda's death, a member of his family had alerted Peel police - the local force in Mississauga - about Duda's behaviour, though Blain did not provide any details. Among the issues likely to be addressed during the inquest is what was, or wasn't, done by the Peel force in the hours prior to Duda's death.
According the SIU, the incident began just after 1 a.m. on April 19, 2010, when both a 911 caller and two officers on patrol noticed Duda driving erratically in the Beaches area.

After a brief car chase - which was called off because of threats to public safety - Duda drove towards the Port Lands area, where he was located by two other officers. While attempting to stop him, Duda struck their police cruiser, then headed towards Cherry and Commissioners Sts.

Police descended on the area and parked their cruisers near the intersection, while another cruiser followed Duda's car with lights and sirens on. According to the police watchdog, some officers drew their pistols, and one had a shot gun. As Duda came to a stop, officers shouted to Duda to show his hands and get out of the car.
Instead, he accelerated towards the officers and struck one, identified Monday as Const. Curtis Hibbert.
Hibbert hit the windshield and rolled off. At nearly the same instance several officers shot at Duda, discharging 32 rounds from their pistols. The officer with a shotgun fired twice.
Hibbert, who is an accomplished gymnast and represented Canada twice at the Olympics, received only minor injuries.

The inquest, expected to last a month, will hear from the officers involved, police training experts, a forensic pathologist and others to discuss questions surrounding actions taken by officers in the lead-up to Duda's death. Among the issues likely to arise is whether police could have employed less lethal force, such as a spike belt, to halt Duda's vehicle.
Duda's psychiatrist and some family members are also scheduled to testify in order to understand more about Duda's state of mind.

According to friends and neighbours, Duda, his parents, wife and sisters immigrated to Canada from Poland more than 15 years ago. Shortly after his death, one neighbour said Duda worked at a Mississauga factory but had gone on a medical disability leave.

The inquest into Duda's death is the latest in a list of probes exploring how Toronto police handle situations involving people suffering from mental illness, and when how officers decide to use lethal force.

This summer, retired Supreme Court Justice Frank Iacobucci released a sweeping report into police use of force; among his numerous recommendations was a shift in police culture that assumed deaths were inevitable. Iacobucci's report was prompted by the July 2013 death of teenager Sammy Yatim, who was shot by James Forcillo, a Toronto police officer now facing a second-degree murder charge and an attempted murder charge in relation to the shooting.
Earlier this year, a coroner's inquest into the police shooting deaths of Reyal Jardine-Douglas, Sylvia Klibingaitis and Michael Eligon made 74 recommendations to avoid similar deaths in the future.

Bergmanis said Duda's family is not currently looking for any specific changes to be made, but hopes the inquest into his death will provide additional pressure to implement the recommendations made during the Jardine-Douglas/Eligon/ Klibingaitis inquest.
"We'll just let the process take its course and hope that that happens," he said.
